entries.why_wrong: You're right that `var`-scoped loop counters cause stale-closure bugs, but swapping `const` for `let` on `field` doesn't touch the actual problem. The `validate` function never even reads `field` — it re-reads `fields[i]`, so the fix has to change what index gets captured, not how `field` is declared.

Object keys aren't the issue here — each field presumably has a distinct `name`, so `validators[field.name]` assigns each validator to its own slot without clobbering earlier ones. The real failure happens later, inside the closure, when it looks up `fields[i]` with a stale index.

Changing the loop to `i <= fields.length` would actually make things worse by reading past the end of the array on the final pass — that's a different class of bug than the one here. The loop bounds are fine; the problem is that the stored function reads `i` only after the loop has already finished running.

Capturing `field` with `const` inside the loop does create a fresh binding each iteration, but that only helps if the closure actually uses it. `validate` ignores `field` entirely and reads `fields[i]` instead, so that fresh per-iteration variable never gets used and the closure still falls victim to `i` being `var`-scoped.
